Lessons.Title: Planning a Pizza Party
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: plan a realistic group meal by identifying fixed and variable quantities, expressing costs using variables and presenting constraints with equations or inequalities. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation based on Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition, Unit 2 Lesson 1, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/1/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher roles: Building On 7.EE.A; Addressing HSA-CED.A.2, HSA-CED.A.3 and HSN-Q.A.2. The source expects students to develop and defend different possible models, rather than impose one unique plan.

Original Edulytiks classroom scenario: each pizza costs $14 and contains enough equal servings for 3 guests; drinks and plates cost a combined $8 regardless of number of guests. Let n be the nonnegative whole number of guests and p the nonnegative whole number of pizzas. Cost C=14p+8 dollars, capacity constraint 3p≥n, and a budget constraint C≤120. If class attendance is at most 24, also require 0≤n≤24. Different assumptions about appetites would change the capacity constraint; state them explicitly.

For 20 guests, seven pizzas provide 21 servings and cost 14×7+8=$106. Six pizzas provide only 18 servings so fail the capacity requirement. Eight pizzas cost 14×8+8=$120 and fit the budget, but nine cost $134 and violate it. No single solution is mathematically compulsory until the objective (least cost, maximum spare food or other preference) is specified.

Modeling activity: with a partner, identify which costs are fixed and which scale with people, write and interpret at least two constraints with inequalities, produce an alternative feasible plan under a changed budget, and explain the strengths and weaknesses of your assumptions. A free-response plan and peer critique are human-scored. A single automatically graded cost result does not establish the source's modelling objective.

Teacher rubric, 0–2 each (8 maximum): correct variable definitions with integer/nonnegative domains, valid expression/equation and at least two inequalities, independently checked feasible plan with units, and justified assumptions with alternative/critique. Never claim an original student party plan or actual restaurant quote was collected if it was not.

V12 source-aligned three-group planning task (all data fictional): given 20 guests, $14 per pizza with 3 servings per pizza, and a fixed $8 for drinks/plates, GROUP A proposes 6 pizzas ($92, only 18 servings, invalid), GROUP B proposes 7 pizzas ($106, 21 servings, valid), GROUP C proposes 8 pizzas ($120, 24 servings, valid). The class budget is $120. Each group states variables n,p, expression C=14p+8, capacity 3p≥n, budget 14p+8≤120 and integer restrictions; a peer must question an assumption before selecting a plan.

V12 warm-up modeling analogue (independently chosen numbers): let m=$9 be a main dish, q be an integer number of $2 side dishes, and T=9+2q. At q=3, T=$15. Explain what each symbol represents and why an equation is a model of one possible meal, not a universal price. Change the day-of-party quantities into variables and identify possible integer/inequality constraints.

The publisher expects collaborative planning with more than one defensible approach. Teacher scores actual student proposals and rationale, not only the numerical cost: 0–2 each for assumptions/variables, expressions and units, valid constraints, and reasoned presentation/critique. Planning discussion remains unverified without learner evidence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Variable versus fixed quantity
KeyConcepts.Definition: A variable can change across possible plans; a fixed parameter stays constant under stated assumptions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name values, meaning and units before forming an expression.
KeyConcepts.Example: p is pizzas (whole number), $14 is price per pizza, $8 is a fixed service charge.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constraint
KeyConcepts.Definition: A limitation restricting acceptable choices, often represented by an inequality.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain every boundary, direction and domain in context.

KeyConcepts.Title: Feasible plan and objective
KeyConcepts.Definition: A feasible solution satisfies all constraints; an optimal plan also depends on a chosen goal.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check all constraints before interpreting a cost as acceptable.
KeyConcepts.Example: With n=20, p=7 and p=8 are feasible; p=6 lacks servings and p=9 exceeds budget.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find minimum feasible pizzas
WorkedExamples.Question: At least how many 3-serving pizzas are required for 20 guests?
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the capacity constraint, require whole pizzas, and check the adjacent integers.
Steps: Define n=20 and nonnegative whole-number p.
Because p must be an integer, the smallest possible p is 7.
Check p=6 yields 18 servings, too few, while p=7 yields 21 servings.
WorkedExamples.Answer: At least 7 pizzas are required under the 3-servings-per-pizza assumption.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check the budget boundary
WorkedExamples.Question: Which plans with 20 guests and 6,7,8,9 pizzas are feasible under $120?
WorkedExamples.Method: Apply capacity and budget inequalities together.
Steps: At p=6, cost 14×6+8=$92 but capacity 18<20, so not feasible.
At p=7, cost $106 and capacity 21, meeting both.
At p=8, cost $120 and capacity 24, meeting both exactly at budget.
At p=9, cost $134, exceeding $120 despite sufficient servings.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Seven or eight pizzas are feasible for 20 guests.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both capacity 3p≥20 and cost 14p+8≤120 are satisfied only by p=7,8 among the four tested.

WorkedExamples.Title: Alter the cost assumption
WorkedExamples.Question: A $6 per-guest drink allowance replaces the $8 fixed service cost; could 7 pizzas serve 20 guests under a $220 budget?
WorkedExamples.Method: Replace the cost model while preserving the capacity constraint.
Steps: New cost model is C=14p+6n, with dollars as units.
Since 218≤220, the plan is feasible; there is only $2 budget margin.
Clarify that drinks now vary with attendance rather than being fixed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, seven pizzas and guest drinks cost $218 under a $220 budget.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both inequalities hold and units are dollars and servings, respectively.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a fractional number of pizzas without a justified sale assumption
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Whole pizzas must be purchased in this scenario.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Apply the nonnegative-integer domain and round the capacity requirement upward.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking cost but not serving capacity
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A cheap plan can leave guests without food.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a particular model as a unique source answer
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The class can choose different menus, prices, assumptions and goals.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the assumptions and explain what makes the plan feasible under them.

SummaryPoints: Define fixed costs, changing quantities and real-world domains before forming a cost expression.
Constraints like 3p≥n and 14p+8≤120 limit feasible plans.
For 20 guests, p=7 costs $106 and p=8 costs $120; both satisfy these particular assumptions.
Authentic modeling and peer critique require a teacher-scored rubric, not only a numeric auto-grade.
